newsitem.title: USA: Rep. Leach opposes mix of commerce and banking.
newsitem.headline: Rep. Leach opposes mix of commerce and banking.

text.p: With the Clinton Administration considering a proposal to allow banks to merge with non-financial companies, House Banking Committee Chairman Jim Leach has reiterated his long time opposition to the idea.
In a letter to Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin dated Jan. 23 released Monday, Leach warned that "efforts to advance too radical a change jeopardize prospects for meaningful reform."

Most in Congress and the administration agree on the need to tear down the 60-year-old laws separating banking and other financial sectors like insurance and securities dealing. But there is little agreement about going further.

Under Secretary of the Treasury John Hawke headed a Treasury Department task force that recommended the administration adopt the more far-reaching plan, allowing banks and other financial services firms to own or be owned by non-financial companies, people familiar with the plan said.
But Leach opposed that approach in his letter and in a banking reform bill he introduced earlier this month.

"America has very few examples of how big, intertwined ownership of companies has brought intelligent, quick-witted and flexible decision making to corporate enterprises," the Iowa Republican wrote to Rubin.
"The nation, it seems to many of us, needs principally to be concerned about building and creating jobs, not consolidating ownership," he added.

A veteran of several previous attempts to overhaul U.S. banking laws, Leach said smaller independent banks, insurance agents and consumer and agriculture groups would also likely oppose mixing banks and non-financial companies. "There is no public support and dubious economic need," he wrote.
And Leach raised a second possible stumbling block on the road to broad financial sector reform.
While most participants in the debate have focused on the commerce and banking issue, Leach said regulatory issues are also unresolved.

"Naturally, the private sector has a great desire for added powers, but little desire for concomitant regulation," Leach wrote. One goal of reform should be "to ensure that the public is protected by a modicum of appropriate regulation."
A spokesman for the Treasury said the department has not yet responded to Leach's letter and declined to comment on the Hawke task force proposal.

Leach also sent the letter to Gene Sperling, Clinton's Assistant for Economic Policy on the National Economic Council, Securities and Exchange Commission chairman Arthur Levitt and Alan Greenspan, chairman of the Federal Reserve Board.
